https://www.dailyadvertiser.com.au/story.text: A court in Croatia has remanded a Ukrainian man who is suspected of involvement in the attacks on the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022 in custody. This marks the start of proceedings regarding the suspect's impending extradition to Germany, the Croatian broadcaster HRT reported. The suspect - described as a scuba diver by German prosecutors who have identified him only as Vladimir Z - was arrested in the early hours on Wednesday in a hotel in the Croatian coastal city of Pula on a European arrest warrant issued by Germany. Matija Milos, the Ukrainian's lawyer, said his client would challenge the impending extradition through legal channels and pursue all available remedies. Under Croatian law, the proceedings - including any appeal - must be concluded within 60 days. The charges against the man include jointly causing an explosion using explosives. Vladimir Z is alleged to have been one of the divers who attached the explosive charges to the pipelines in the North Sea. The explosions - described by Russia and European countries as sabotage - damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, a vital route for Russian gas exports to Europe, as well as the Nord Stream 2 branch, which had yet to enter service. According to the Croatian police, the suspect was arrested at tourist accommodation in a resort on the southern outskirts of Pula. The resort is also hosting a Hollywood film crew which is currently filming the Nord Stream attacks as a fictional political thriller. Directed by the US director Doug Liman, the film features Hollywood stars Sean Penn and Adrien Brody. The suspect is reported to have been staying in Pula as part of this film crew, registered at the accommodation under a false name. According to the London Times newspaper, he was working on the production as a consultant. The man was previously arrested in Poland at the end of September last year, also based on a European arrest warrant issued in Germany. However, the government in Poland, a close ally of Ukraine, refused to extradite him. It is considered unlikely that Croatia will follow suit. with Reuters Australian Associated Press

Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian BBC The Archers cast ‘angry’ at BBC decision to scrap new Birmingham studio Ben Norris says cost-cutting measure that means show will be recorded outside its home city risks ‘extraordinary burden’ for crew Michael Savage Media editor Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.12 EDT First published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A cast member of The Archers has said its actors have been angered by the BBC’s decision to axe the show’s new studio, in a move that could lead to it being recorded away from its home in Birmingham. Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer in the world’s longest-running soap opera, said the decision risked having a real impact on the quality of the show and placing an “extraordinary burden” on its crew. Norris told the Guardian that current plans, which would involve production staff working in a separate location to the actors recording the show, represented “classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer”. “This isn’t us actors being averse to change,” he said. “It’s very much us wanting to stand in solidarity with our colleagues in production, us wanting to ensure the continued highest quality of the programme for the listeners, the continued heritage of the show, its connection to Birmingham , and also for the BBC not to go back on many promises it made to the region. View image in fullscreen Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer, said the actors wanted to stand in solidarity with colleagues in production. Photograph: Steve Ullathorne “It’s a combination of all those things that has left us feeling as angry as we are.” Staff were informed last week that the BBC, as part of its £500m cost-cutting drive, had ditched plans for a new radio drama theatre at the Tea Factory in Digbeth, the corporation’s new Birmingham headquarters. While production staff will still move to the facility, the broadcaster is now looking for an existing UK studio where the show could be recorded. The West Midlands is included in the search, but there is no guarantee The Archers will be recorded in the region in which it has been based since its launch 75 years ago. Cast members met on Monday to discuss the announcement. Norris said there were practical problems with the new plan, including the need for last-minute script discussions and specific facilities. “The Archers is recorded in a very specific way that is unlike almost all other audio drama,” he said. “There are very few other studios that have those facilities, and none that are up to the same specifications as our current setup. “[The current studio setup] would need transporting, building and striking with any new space we travel to, placing an extraordinary burden on the technical team and incurring extra financial drain. “I also think it’s a totally false economy. I’ve been told that the additional cost of shipping those people to wherever we ended up would cancel out what it costs to build the new studio within five years, so it’s classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer at all.” He said that while actors were based in different places, there was a “big Midlands connection within the cast – either people who grew up or trained there or people who live there now”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history Read more “For day players, of which the Archers has many – coming in to play somebody’s midwife, somebody’s mechanic – those roles often go to local actors and should go to local actors because it’s one of the places that people can start their careers,” he said. “It’s the same for the writing team and the production team. “This decision flies completely in the face of the BBC and the government’s commitment to pursue as much regionality as possible and to have culture and the economy thriving in every postcode.” Norris feared listeners would eventually notice the impact. “We’re worried about the sustainability of this way of working,” he said. “We are worried about the relationship between cast and crew, but also their energy levels, their wellbeing … Maybe we’d get away with it for a bit, but we think at some point the show would suffer and the listeners would perceive that.” The performing arts union Equity has said it will oppose the BBC’s plans. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said hemet the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, on Wednesday to explore opportunities to continue to record the show in the region once it left Birmingham. Photograph: Michel Euler/AP View image in fullscreen Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities in France. Photograph: Michel Euler/AP Bonds French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests Phillip Inman Senior economics writer Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.17 EDT First published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) , issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks. Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living. Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics , sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges. No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024 . The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending. France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action. International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies. “The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.” Explore more on these topics Bonds Eurozone France Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors Bank governor urges John Healey to use budget to allay market fears amid bond turmoil Why are French police so violent? https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: WARSAW — NATO must modernize its military infrastructure to move forces and equipment from Western to Eastern Europe “where we would expect any future conflict,” U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said Monday. Speaking on a panel at the Warsaw Security Forum, Whitaker’s comments came as Washington reviews its military presence on the continent — with the ambassador saying that Europe ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic priorities, behind homeland security, the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific. He pointed to outdated military bases, fuel supply chains and agreements governing the stationing of American troops in Europe as areas requiring attention under the ongoing U.S. force posture and basing review. Advertisement Advertisement He emphasized the importance of military mobility and “moving things from the west to the east,” citing discussions with EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. European officials warn that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country by the end of the decade. Whitaker did not announce any decisions to relocate or withdraw American forces. He nevertheless made clear that Washington is reassessing its global commitments to avoid spreading its military resources too thin. “Superpowers and great global powers have mostly had challenges when they get overextended,” Whitaker said, adding that U.S. President Donald Trump wants allies to become “capable and not dependent.” “The United States isn’t stepping back. We’re just asking you to step forward,” he said. Whitaker also criticized countries that are falling short of their defense-spending commitments. He said he had recently delivered a “very strong message” to political leaders in Czechia. The country’s defense spending for this year is approximately 1.8% of GDP, falling short of NATO’s current 2% benchmark. Advertisement Advertisement European governments must continue strengthening their armed forces, he argued, warning that the continent still lacks many of the capabilities it needs to defend itself. Kubilius, meanwhile, stressed the need to reduce Europe’s military dependence on Washington, highlighting EU efforts to develop its own drone defenses, satellite communications and surveillance capabilities. Polish presidential adviser Marcin Przydacz, also on the panel, urged Western European allies to accelerate defense spending while emphasizing that NATO, rather than the EU, must remain responsible for Europe’s collective defense.
